name: Jamal Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jamal. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go down the decline at Kestrel at six, that's the gold mine past the river bridge, about nine hundred metres underground. I drive a loader, what we call a bogger, scooping broken rock from the stopes after the blast and tramming it to the trucks. It's hot, it's loud, and you wear the vibration home in your back. But I like the crew. We have tea at the crib room at ten and argue about football, and for half an hour nobody is boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how did you come to be underground?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Late, very late. I ran a small grocery on Station Road for nineteen years, and the supermarket that opened by the highway finished it. When I closed I owed the wholesaler money, which I'm still paying back, so we have almost nothing saved. Kestrel was hiring trainee operators three years ago and they took me at fifty-five. I'm still the one the shift boss watches when the stope is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. A quiet few years would be a gift. I've already lost one business to something bigger and cheaper, so I don't need a second lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the crib room I'd say good, maybe now they'll stop sending us those videos about the mine of the future. Then we'd go back to arguing about football. In the family chat I'd send a thumbs up and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the plateau doesn't fix my real problem, which is that I'm slow in the tight stopes and the shift boss knows it. I still owe the wholesaler about 4,000 from my old grocery shop, and we have maybe two weeks of money. If the gold price drops and they trim the crews, the newest and slowest goes first, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my trainer for extra practice time in the tight stopes, on my own time if I have to. I'd keep paying the wholesaler 200 a month and aim to clear it in two years. And we'd go without the trip to see Priya's sister again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a familiar way. It's the shop feeling, watching the till and hoping nobody notices you're struggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it look like when the shift boss watches you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Doyle stands at the stope entrance with his arms folded when I'm tramming. Twice this year the shift boss put a younger driver in my seat on the loader when the tunnel got tight. Nobody says anything, but everyone sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son his father's fine and his job at the call centre is the one to look after. Arjun's 31 and he still worries about me more than he should. I wouldn't mention the debt, because he'd try to pay it.

In the family chat I'd send **a thumbs up** and nothing else.

I still owe the wholesaler **about 4,000**, and we have maybe two weeks of money.
If crews are trimmed, **the newest and slowest** goes first, and that's me.

Puts off **the trip** to see Priya's sister again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking jobs first, robots slowly. Answering customers is on that list, and that's my son Arjun's whole job. Underground, the loaders would carry on for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say the robots are slow in this one, so the loaders underground are fine for now, and the company should train older crews for the new systems too. In the family chat I'd tell Arjun to start looking around, gently. I wouldn't post anything anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my loader holds for a few years, but the surface room where they run loaders by remote control is growing, and they'll want young operators for it. If they move the good young drivers upstairs and bring in a couple of remote loaders, the crews shrink and I'm still the slow one. And if Arjun's call centre cuts staff, he moves back in, which we can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the tele-remote training the first week, even though I doubt they'd pick me. I'd ask Arjun to teach me the AI tools properly on Sunday afternoons. I'd keep paying the wholesaler, and save about fifty a month on top by not buying lunch at the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a small door open. I'd rather knock on it and be told no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put your name down if you think they won't pick you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd hate myself if I didn't try. With my grocery shop I waited too long to change anything, and the supermarket didn't wait for me. If they say no, at least Mr Doyle knows I asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Arjun moving back in mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another mouth on two small wages and a debt. Priya would be happy to have him home, and I'd be happy too, for about a week. Then I'd be doing sums at the kitchen table at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the screens go first and the hands after. That's the opposite of what I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union meeting I'd say the remote control room is the first thing the computers take, so stop telling us to retrain for it. I'd say the loaders underground still need us until 2031, and that's the time to win a proper deal. In the family group I'd just send something like 'don't worry, Dad's still digging'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the joke's on the young lads. The warm office with the screens on the surface, that's thinking work, and in 2028 the computer runs those loaders by itself. My job in the stope, scraping the walls, lasts three more years. I'd be 63 when the robots come, two years short of my pension at 65, with nothing saved because all the money's gone to the wholesaler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift and clear the wholesaler debt by the end of 2028, a year early. Then whatever we used to pay him goes straight into savings, maybe 200 a month for three years. I'd go to the union and ask for an age-based bridge for anyone within five years of the pension. And I wouldn't bother with the tele-remote course, because it's a course for a job that's going first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lost. I've seen a business die before, and this time at least I can see the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years short of the pension. How would you and Priya cover that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya cooks at the school, that's hands-on too, so she might go the same year as me. We'd need the 7,000 or so we'd saved from 2028 to 2031, and maybe Arjun would help. I'd hate asking my son for money. I did it once with the shop and I still remember his face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said before that you'd hate yourself if you didn't try. Does that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, but the trying changes. In the slow picture I'd try for the remote job. Here the smart move is to stay the best loader driver in the stope for three years and save every coin, because the remote control room job disappears before my underground loader job does.

think: The surface screens are **thinking work** that goes in 2028, while my stope job lasts three more years.

fieldNote: Jamal noticed the surface control room job he hoped for is **the thinking work** that goes first.

The **two years** between the robots and his pension are the gap he can't yet cover.

steps.text: Clear the wholesaler debt by the end of 2028 with overtime shifts
Ask the union for an age-based bridge for workers near the pension
Stay on the underground loader at Kestrel and skip the remote course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be sixty-six. Pension at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union that five years is time to get it right, and I'd want every worker over sixty protected in writing. At crib I'd say I might be the lucky one for once. The young lads would laugh, but they'd have to think about it longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, for once the timing might be on my side, which never happens to me. The computers take the control room in 2031, the robots come down the decline in 2034, and I'm out at 65 in 2033. I'd still be watching every month in case the company moves early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into clearing the shop debt in the first year. Then I'd save what I can, maybe 150 a month, and I'd keep practising with the AI programs Arjun showed me, half an hour in the evenings, because the paperwork side of retiring will all be online. I'd stay on the loader until my last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a light at the end of the decline for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even if you made it to your pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya. She'd be 62 in 2034 when the robots came, and the school kitchen might not need her. I'd be retired with a small pension and she'd be out of work. We'd manage, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want the tele-remote course in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. In 2031 the computer does that job, and I'd be two years from my pension. Better to be the steady old loader driver than the slowest one on the screens.

I might be **the lucky one** for once.

I'd still **watch every month** in case the company moves early.

Stays **on the loader** until his last day.

S3.quote: For once the timing might be on my side, which never happens to me.
fieldNote: This timeline lets Jamal **retire a year before** the robots, and he can hardly believe his luck.
His remaining worry is **his wife's kitchen job**, which would go after he retires.
He drops **the remote course** because the computers take that job first.

steps.text: Clear the shop debt in year one, then save about 150 a month
Practise the AI programs Arjun set up for half an hour each evening
Stay on the Kestrel underground loader until his pension at 65

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039? I'd be long retired. It's Arjun's problem then, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union this is the picture for the young crews, and they should start planning now. I'd tell them what happened to my shop, waiting too long. Ten years goes faster than you think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd retire in 2033 and the robots come six years later. What I'd think about is Arjun, who works in a call centre, and that's exactly the thinking work the computers take in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, clear the debt and start saving properly for the first time. I'd cut the money I send my brother back home down to half, to build something. And I'd keep learning the AI tools a little, so I can help Arjun when his turn comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sad for my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son not to wait the way I did with the shop. He's 31 and he's got ten years, which is more than I had. If he starts something hands-on now, he gets those extra three years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss when you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crib at ten, arguing about football. Nobody's boss for half an hour. I don't think a robot will miss that.

Ten years goes **faster than you think**, as I learned with my shop.
think: I'd be fine, **retiring in 2033**, six years before the robots.
I'd think about **Arjun's call centre job**, exactly the thinking work the computers take in 2036.

fieldNote: With the long timeline Jamal's own future is settled, and his concern moves to **his son**.
He uses the card's three-year gap to advise that **hands-on work** buys time.
The lesson of **his failed shop** runs through everything he says.

steps.text: Keep driving the Kestrel loader until retiring in 2033
Clear the debt, then save properly and halve the money sent to his brother
Keep learning the AI tools so he can help Arjun later

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the robots would come two years before my pension, and I'd have only just cleared the shop debt. What would help is redundancy pay that looks at your age, not how long you've been at the mine, and the government paying off debts like mine for people over fifty-five who lose their work. Just let us reach the pension without a hole in our pockets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who came to mining late, like me. We're not slow because we're stupid, we're slow because we started at fifty-five, and nobody counts that. Ask the company why it's always us they look at first.

headlineQuote: We're not slow because we're stupid, we're slow because we started at fifty-five, and nobody counts that.
portrait: Jamal Gupta, 58, drives **an underground loader** at the Kestrel gold mine, which he joined at fifty-five after his shop failed.
He still owes **the old wholesaler**, so he and his wife Priya, a school cook, have almost nothing saved.
In a plateau he's **anxious**, because he's slow in the tight tunnels and would go first in any crew cut.
Steady change keeps him **anxious**: his son's call centre job is exposed, and he'd still try remote training.
Fast AGI worries him about **the gap** before his pension; with more time he expects to retire first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach his underground job two years before his pension.
He'd only just have paid off **the shop's debt**.
whatWouldHelp: **Redundancy pay** based on age rather than years at the mine.
Government help to **clear debts** for older workers who lose their jobs, so they reach the pension.
